column1: What is the main purpose of a database index?
column2:
Provide an efficient access path to the required data.
For example, an index on CustomerID can find one customer's orders without reading pages for unrelated customers. The benefit depends on the query and data.
Review source

column1: Why can adding nonclustered indexes to a SQL Server table make inserts slower?
column2:
Data changes also require maintenance of affected indexes.
Inserting an order writes the row and adds entries to its applicable indexes. Updates can also touch index entries, so each extra index needs a read benefit.
Review source

column1: What extra storage does a nonclustered index need beyond the base table?
column2:
Space for a separate index structure.
The extra structure holds indexed values and row locators. Included columns can make it larger even though they are not part of its search key.
Review source

column1: Which index storage format generally suits transactional queries that retrieve individual records?
column2:
Rowstore.
Rows keep their columns together in rowstore storage. That fits a lookup by order ID that needs several values from one row.
Review source

column1: In a clustered rowstore index, what does the key order organize at the leaf level?
column2:
The table's data rows at its leaf level.
The leaf is where the clustered index holds the full data rows. Key order organizes access, but only ORDER BY guarantees the sequence returned by a query.
Review source

column1: Why can a clustered rowstore index help range queries on its key?
column2:
Rows with nearby key values are organized together.
A seek can start near the low key and scan until the high key. It need not read key ranges outside the requested interval.
Review source

column1: Why can a narrow clustered key save space in a table's nonclustered indexes?
column2:
It reduces index storage, I/O, and memory overhead.
The clustered key travels with nonclustered entries as their row locator. A wide key therefore takes space in more than one index.
Review source

column1: Why favor a stable clustered index key whose values do not change?
column2:
Changing it also requires updating row locators in nonclustered indexes.
An update to the clustered key can change how every nonclustered index locates that row. A stable key avoids that extra write work.
Review source

column1: What do SQL Server nonclustered rowstore index entries use to find their base-table rows?
column2:
Its key entries contain row locators.
The locator is the clustered key on a clustered rowstore table. On a heap, it identifies the physical row instead.
Review source

column1: What must a nonclustered index contain to cover a particular query?
column2:
It contains every column that the query references.
For a query that filters on Category and returns Price, an index can cover it with Category as a key and Price as an included column.
Review source

column1: A nonclustered index covers a query on a clustered table. Which extra fetch does that avoid?
column2:
A key lookup into the clustered index.
Without coverage, SQL Server can use the clustered key to fetch a missing value for each match. Coverage makes those extra fetches unnecessary.
Review source

column1: What makes SQL Server choose an available index or a scan for a particular query?
column2:
The query optimizer's cost-based access-path choice.
The optimizer estimates the cost of the available paths for the current query. An index that helps a selective lookup can be ignored for a broad query.
Review source

column1: Why can a table scan be efficient when a query returns most rows?
column2:
Reading the table directly can cost less than many indexed lookups.
When most rows qualify, a seek followed by many row lookups can read more pages than a scan. Seek and scan labels alone do not measure efficiency.
Review source

column1: What clause guarantees a requested query-result order, even when a clustered index exists?
column2:
ORDER BY.
An execution plan can read or combine rows in an order unrelated to the clustered key. Add a unique tie breaker to ORDER BY if tied rows need a stable order.
Review source

column1: Which workload is a strong fit for columnstore indexes?
column2:
Large analytical scans and aggregations.
A query that totals sales over millions of rows often reads only a few columns. Columnstore can read less data than a matching scan of full rows.
Review source

column1: A query needs only Amount and OrderDate. How can a columnstore scan avoid reading other columns?
column2:
It reads the required columns without reading every column's data.
Columnstore can read the amount and date segments for a sales total without reading product descriptions. Each rowgroup stores its columns separately.
Review source

column1: Why do columnstore indexes often compress data well?
column2:
Values within a column often have similar or repeated patterns.
Similar values, such as a repeated status code, can use less space when stored together. Compression gains vary with the distribution of the values.
Review source

column1: What does a clustered columnstore index store, as opposed to a nonclustered columnstore index?
column2:
It is the primary storage structure for the entire table.
A clustered columnstore is the table's storage, not a secondary copy of selected fields. The deltastore holds some rows until they enter compressed rowgroups.
Review source

column1: Which index adds column-oriented analytics while preserving an existing rowstore table?
column2:
A nonclustered columnstore index.
Add a nonclustered columnstore to support analytics over selected columns without replacing the base rowstore. Each write can still require index maintenance.
Review source

column1: Where do small inserts into a clustered columnstore table initially accumulate?
column2:
In the deltastore.
The deltastore holds rows in row-oriented groups. SQL Server can compress a group into columnar storage later without making new rows unavailable in the meantime.
Review source

column1: What does the columnstore tuple-mover do after a delta rowgroup closes?
column2:
It compresses them into columnstore rowgroups.
The tuple-mover handles closed delta rowgroups in the background. Until it compresses a group, that group remains in rowstore format.
Review source

column1: Which two storage areas can supply visible rows in a clustered columnstore scan?
column2:
The compressed columnstore and the deltastore.
The engine combines visible rows from both storage areas. A newly inserted row can appear in results even before its delta rowgroup is compressed.
Review source

column1: Why can many small compressed rowgroups hurt columnstore efficiency?
column2:
They generally achieve poorer compression than fuller rowgroups.
Many small groups have more per-group overhead and fewer values to compress together. Check rowgroup statistics before assuming an index rebuild will help.
Review source

column1: What does SQL Server do first when you delete a row in a compressed clustered columnstore rowgroup?
column2:
It is marked deleted rather than immediately removed from compressed storage.
SQL Server records the deletion separately and filters the row out of query results. The compressed data can still occupy space until maintenance removes it.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view reports columnstore rowgroup states, row counts, and storage sizes?
column2:
sys.dm_db_column_store_row_group_physical_stats.
Use the view to compare row count, deleted rows, and size across groups. That helps distinguish undersized rowgroups from groups with many deleted rows.
Review source

column1: Which ALTER INDEX operation can combine eligible small compressed columnstore rowgroups without a full rebuild?
column2:
REORGANIZE.
REORGANIZE can combine compressed groups that meet its rules. A small row count does not guarantee that any particular pair will merge.
Review source

column1: Which statement rebuilds the columnstore index CCI_SalesHistory on dbo.SalesHistory?
column2:
ALTER INDEX CCI_SalesHistory ON dbo.SalesHistory REBUILD;
REBUILD recreates the index. It does more work than a reorganization and can require more resources, so match the operation to the maintenance goal.
Review source

column1: What execution mode processes multiple rows together and is optimized for columnstore analytics?
column2:
Batch mode execution.
Batch mode processes groups of rows to reduce overhead per row. It is common with columnstore, but eligible rowstore plans can also use batch mode.
Review source
